slides.title: Confidentiality
slides.teach: Confidentiality means keeping information private from people who are not authorized to see it.

course.learn: Confidentiality means keeping information private from people who are not authorized to see it.

breakdown.explanation: Only approved people should be able to see sensitive information.
Encryption, passwords, MFA, file permissions, and access controls.

course.why: Unauthorized disclosure can expose credentials, personal data, financial records, and other sensitive information.
course.example: An employee accidentally sends customer Social Security numbers to the wrong recipient.
course.exam: If the scenario emphasizes exposure, disclosure, unauthorized viewing, or leaked information, think confidentiality.
course.check_q: A hacker reads unencrypted employee credentials. Which CIA principle is affected?

slides.title: Integrity
slides.teach: Integrity means keeping information accurate and protected from unauthorized changes.

course.learn: Integrity means keeping information accurate and protected from unauthorized changes.

breakdown.explanation: The data should remain correct and trustworthy.
Hashing, digital signatures, checksums, permissions, and version controls.

course.why: Security decisions can become unreliable if data is altered without authorization.
course.example: An attacker changes employees' direct-deposit bank account numbers in payroll.
course.exam: If data was modified, altered, tampered with, or can no longer be trusted, think integrity.
course.check_q: Malware modifies financial records without permission. Which CIA principle is affected?

slides.title: Availability
slides.teach: Availability means making sure authorized users can access systems and data when needed.

course.learn: Availability means making sure authorized users can access systems and data when needed.

breakdown.explanation: The system must be usable when legitimate users need it.
Backups, redundancy, failover, disaster recovery, load balancing, and UPS systems.

course.why: A secure system still fails its users if it is unavailable when needed.
course.example: A DDoS attack overwhelms a website so legitimate customers cannot connect.
course.exam: If users cannot access a system, application, service, or data, think availability.
course.check_q: A database server fails and employees cannot access records. Which CIA principle is affected?

slides.title: Authentication
slides.teach: Authentication means proving that you are who you claim to be.

course.learn: Authentication means proving that you are who you claim to be.

breakdown.explanation: Prove your identity.
Passwords, fingerprints, Face ID, smart cards, security tokens, and MFA.

course.why: Identity must be verified before a system can make an informed access decision.
course.example: A user enters a password and MFA code before signing in.
course.exam: Authentication answers: Who are you?
course.check_q: A user scans a fingerprint before signing in. Which AAA function is this?

slides.title: Authorization
slides.teach: Authorization means determining what an authenticated user or system is allowed to access or do.

course.learn: Authorization means determining what an authenticated user or system is allowed to access or do.

breakdown.explanation: I know who you are. Now what are you allowed to do?
Read/write permissions, role-based access, administrator privileges, and application permissions.

course.why: Different authenticated users can require different levels of access.
course.example: A student may view grades, while a professor may enter or modify grades.
course.exam: Authorization answers: What can you do?
course.check_q: A signed-in user can read a file but cannot edit it. Which AAA function determines this?

slides.title: Accounting
slides.teach: Accounting means recording and tracking what users or systems do.

course.learn: Accounting means recording and tracking what users or systems do.

breakdown.explanation: Keep a record of activity.
Login records, audit logs, session activity, file-access logs, timestamps, and resource usage.

course.why: Accounting supports investigations, auditing, troubleshooting, and accountability.
course.example: A log records when a user signed in, which files were opened, what changed, and when the user logged out.
course.exam: Accounting answers: What did you do?
course.check_q: A system records every file an administrator accessed. Which AAA function is this?

slides.title: Authenticating People
slides.teach: Authenticating people means verifying the identity of a human user.

course.learn: Authenticating people means verifying the identity of a human user.

breakdown.explanation: Prove that this person really is who they claim to be.
Passwords, PINs, biometrics, smart cards, security tokens, and MFA.

course.why: Human identities must be validated before access can be trusted.
course.example: An employee scans a fingerprint and enters a PIN before accessing a sensitive system.
course.exam: Look for a human user proving identity with knowledge, possession, biometric, or multiple factors.
course.check_q: An employee uses a fingerprint and PIN to sign in. What is being authenticated?

slides.title: Authenticating Systems
slides.teach: Authenticating systems means verifying the identity of a device, server, application, or service.

course.learn: Authenticating systems means verifying the identity of a device, server, application, or service.

breakdown.explanation: Prove that this computer or service is legitimate.
Digital certificates, machine certificates, cryptographic keys, service credentials, and mutual authentication.

course.why: Systems also need trusted identities so devices and services do not communicate with impostors.
course.example: A client verifies a server's certificate before establishing a secure connection.
course.exam: Look for certificates, machine identities, service identities, or systems verifying each other.
course.check_q: A client validates a server certificate before connecting. What is being authenticated?

slides.title: Authorization Models
slides.teach: Authorization models are methods used to determine who or what receives access to specific resources.

course.learn: Authorization models are methods used to determine who or what receives access to specific resources.

breakdown.explanation: They define how permissions are decided.
Role-based access control uses roles; attribute-based access control uses attributes and context; rule-based access uses defined rules.

course.why: Organizations need repeatable models for assigning and enforcing access permissions.
course.example: Everyone assigned to the HR role automatically receives access to the payroll application.
course.exam: If the question asks how permissions are assigned or what criteria determine access, think authorization model.
course.check_q: Access to payroll is automatically granted to members of the HR role. What concept is being demonstrated?
course.check_a: An authorization model, specifically role-based access.

slides.title: Gap Analysis
slides.teach: Gap analysis compares an organization's current security state with its desired or required security state.

course.learn: Gap analysis compares an organization's current security state with its desired or required security state.

breakdown.explanation: Where are we now, where should we be, and what is missing?
Current state, desired state, identified gaps, and a plan to close those gaps.

course.why: Gap analysis identifies deficiencies that must be addressed to meet security goals or requirements.
course.example: Policy requires MFA for every administrator, but an assessment finds that only 60% of administrator accounts use MFA.
course.exam: Look for current state versus desired state, missing controls, deficiencies, or what must improve.
course.check_q: A company compares its current controls with a required security baseline to identify what is missing. What is this?

slides.title: Zero Trust
slides.teach: Zero Trust is a security approach in which no user, device, or connection is automatically trusted, even if it is already inside the network.

course.learn: Zero Trust is a security approach in which no user, device, or connection is automatically trusted, even if it is already inside the network.

breakdown.explanation: Never trust automatically. Always verify.
MFA, least privilege, device health checks, continuous evaluation, microsegmentation, and context-based access.

course.why: Attackers may already be inside a network, so network location alone should not establish trust.
course.example: An employee is on the corporate network but still must satisfy identity and device checks before reaching a sensitive application.
course.exam: Remember: never trust automatically; always verify.
course.check_q: Internal users must be verified before every sensitive request. Which security model is this?

slides.title: Control Plane
slides.teach: The Zero Trust control plane evaluates context and makes access decisions.

course.learn: The Zero Trust control plane evaluates context and makes access decisions.

breakdown.explanation: The brain that decides whether access should be allowed, denied, or restricted.
Policy Engine, Policy Administrator, adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, and policy-driven access control.

course.why: Separating decision-making from traffic enforcement allows access decisions to be continuously evaluated.
course.example: A Zero Trust system evaluates user identity, device condition, and policy before deciding whether a request may proceed.
course.exam: Control plane = decides.
course.check_q: Which Zero Trust plane is responsible for making access decisions?

slides.title: Adaptive Identity
slides.teach: Adaptive identity changes authentication or access requirements based on risk and context.

course.learn: Adaptive identity changes authentication or access requirements based on risk and context.

breakdown.explanation: The amount of proof required can change when the situation becomes riskier.
Location, device condition, time, user behavior, and risk level.

course.why: A fixed authentication requirement may not be sufficient for every risk level.
course.example: A user normally signs in from Washington but suddenly signs in from another country, so the system requires additional authentication.
course.exam: Adaptive identity = authentication or access requirements change with context and risk.
course.check_q: A login from an unusual location triggers additional verification. Which Zero Trust concept is this?

slides.title: Threat Scope Reduction
slides.teach: Threat scope reduction limits how much damage an attacker can cause if an account, device, or workload is compromised.

course.learn: Threat scope reduction limits how much damage an attacker can cause if an account, device, or workload is compromised.

breakdown.explanation: Limit the blast radius.
Least privilege, segmentation, restricted permissions, and limiting lateral movement.

course.why: Compromise is less damaging when access is tightly limited.
course.example: A compromised employee account can reach only one required application instead of the entire internal network.
course.exam: Think least privilege, segmentation, or limiting the impact of compromise.
course.check_q: A company limits each account to only the systems required for its job to reduce damage from compromise. Which concept applies?

slides.title: Policy-driven Access Control
slides.teach: Policy-driven access control makes access decisions according to defined security policies.

course.learn: Policy-driven access control makes access decisions according to defined security policies.

breakdown.explanation: Rules decide whether the request is allowed.
Policies can consider role, device health, location, resource sensitivity, time, and other context.

course.why: Consistent policy evaluation supports Zero Trust's requirement to verify every request.
course.example: Company policy blocks access to financial records from unmanaged devices.
course.exam: If access is allowed or denied because a defined policy condition was met, think policy-driven access control.
course.check_q: Access to sensitive data is denied from unmanaged devices because of company policy. What concept is this?

slides.title: Policy Engine
slides.teach: The Policy Engine evaluates information and determines whether access should be granted.

course.learn: The Policy Engine evaluates information and determines whether access should be granted.

breakdown.explanation: Should this request be allowed?
Identity, device posture, policy, context, and risk information can contribute to the decision.

course.why: The Policy Engine is the decision-making component of Zero Trust access.
course.example: A component analyzes identity, device health, and policy and decides to allow a request.
course.exam: Policy Engine = decides.
course.check_q: Which Zero Trust component determines whether a request should be allowed?

slides.title: Policy Administrator
slides.teach: The Policy Administrator carries out the Policy Engine's decision by establishing, changing, or terminating the connection through the enforcement mechanism.

course.learn: The Policy Administrator carries out the Policy Engine's decision by establishing, changing, or terminating the connection through the enforcement mechanism.

breakdown.explanation: The Policy Engine decides; the Policy Administrator makes that decision happen.
It communicates the decision so access can be established or removed.

course.why: The decision must be translated into an action that can be enforced.
course.example: The Policy Engine approves a request, and another component coordinates creation of the permitted connection.
course.exam: Policy Administrator = executes the Policy Engine's decision.
course.check_q: Which component acts on the Policy Engine's decision to establish or end access?

slides.title: Data Plane
slides.teach: The Zero Trust data plane is where subjects communicate with and use protected resources after policy decisions are enforced.

course.learn: The Zero Trust data plane is where subjects communicate with and use protected resources after policy decisions are enforced.

breakdown.explanation: This is where the actual connection and data traffic occur.
Subject/system communication and the Policy Enforcement Point operate in the data plane.

course.why: The control plane decides; the data plane carries the permitted communication.
course.example: After access is approved, a user's traffic passes through the enforcement point to the application.
course.exam: Data plane = actual access and communication.
course.check_q: Which Zero Trust plane carries the permitted communication to the resource?

slides.title: Implicit Trust Zones
slides.teach: Implicit trust zones are areas where users or devices are trusted automatically because of their location or network position.

course.learn: Implicit trust zones are areas where users or devices are trusted automatically because of their location or network position.

breakdown.explanation: You're inside, so you're trusted—the assumption Zero Trust tries to remove.
Traditional internal network trust is a common example.

course.why: Zero Trust seeks to reduce or eliminate automatic trust based solely on network location.
course.example: An old network design assumes every device on the internal LAN is trusted without further verification.
course.exam: Implicit trust = automatic trust based on location; Zero Trust minimizes it.
course.check_q: An internal network automatically trusts any connected device. What Zero Trust concern is this?

slides.title: Subject/System
slides.teach: In Zero Trust, the subject is the user, device, application, or service requesting access, and the system is the protected resource being accessed.

course.learn: In Zero Trust, the subject is the user, device, application, or service requesting access, and the system is the protected resource being accessed.

breakdown.explanation: Subject wants access; system has the resource.
A user's laptop can be the subject and a payroll application can be the system/resource.

course.why: Understanding who is requesting access and what resource is targeted is necessary for policy evaluation.
course.example: An employee laptop requests access to a payroll server.
course.exam: Subject = requester; system/resource = destination being requested.
course.check_q: A laptop requests access to a payroll server. Which one is the subject?

slides.title: Policy Enforcement Point
slides.teach: The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) is the component that actually enforces the access decision.

course.learn: The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) is the component that actually enforces the access decision.

breakdown.explanation: The gatekeeper.
It can allow, deny, or terminate connections according to policy decisions.

course.why: A Zero Trust decision has no effect unless something enforces it at the point of access.
course.example: After a request is denied, the PEP blocks the user's connection to the application.
course.exam: PEP = enforces.
course.check_q: Which Zero Trust component actually allows or blocks the connection?

slides.title: Bollards
slides.teach: Bollards are strong physical posts or barriers placed around facilities to stop or redirect vehicles.

course.learn: Bollards are strong physical posts or barriers placed around facilities to stop or redirect vehicles.

breakdown.explanation: Vehicle blockers.
Steel posts, concrete posts, and protective vehicle barriers.

course.why: Bollards protect entrances, buildings, and pedestrian areas from vehicle intrusion.
course.example: A data center installs reinforced steel posts in front of its entrance to prevent vehicles from reaching the doors.
course.exam: Bollards = stop vehicles.
course.check_q: Which physical control is specifically designed to stop vehicles from reaching a building?

slides.title: Access Control Vestibule
slides.teach: An access control vestibule is a small secured area with two controlled doors used to regulate entry into a protected space.

course.learn: An access control vestibule is a small secured area with two controlled doors used to regulate entry into a protected space.

breakdown.explanation: One door closes before the next opens.
Two-door vestibules and mantrap-style entry areas.

course.why: The vestibule helps prevent tailgating and unauthorized entry.
course.example: A user badges through the first door and must wait for it to close before the second door unlocks.
course.exam: Access control vestibule = two controlled doors.
course.check_q: Which control uses two doors so one closes before the other opens?

slides.title: Fencing
slides.teach: Fencing is a physical barrier used to define and protect a perimeter.

course.learn: Fencing is a physical barrier used to define and protect a perimeter.

breakdown.explanation: Keep unauthorized people away from the protected area.
Chain-link fencing, anti-climb fencing, and other perimeter barriers.

course.why: Fencing increases distance and difficulty for unauthorized physical access.
course.example: A facility installs anti-climb fencing around its entire property boundary.
course.exam: Fencing = perimeter protection.
course.check_q: Which physical control primarily protects the perimeter of a property?

slides.title: Video Surveillance
slides.teach: Video surveillance uses cameras to monitor and record activity around protected areas.

course.learn: Video surveillance uses cameras to monitor and record activity around protected areas.

breakdown.explanation: See and record what happens.
CCTV, security cameras, recorded video, and monitored camera feeds.

course.why: Video can deter intruders, detect activity, and provide evidence after an incident.
course.example: Security personnel review recorded camera footage to identify who entered a server room.
course.exam: Video surveillance = see and record.
course.check_q: Which physical control provides recorded visual evidence of activity?

slides.title: Security Guard
slides.teach: A security guard is a person who monitors and protects a physical location.

course.learn: A security guard is a person who monitors and protects a physical location.

breakdown.explanation: Human physical security.
Checking identification, patrolling, monitoring entrances, and responding to incidents.

course.why: Human guards can make contextual decisions and respond to events that automated controls may not handle.
course.example: A guard checks visitor identification before allowing entry to a restricted facility.
course.exam: Security guard = human protection.
course.check_q: Which physical control uses a person to verify visitors and respond to incidents?

slides.title: Access Badge
slides.teach: An access badge is a physical credential used to identify a person and control entry to a protected area.

course.learn: An access badge is a physical credential used to identify a person and control entry to a protected area.

breakdown.explanation: A physical access credential.
RFID badge, smart badge, proximity card, and employee ID credential.

course.why: Badges help restrict physical entry to authorized personnel.
course.example: An employee taps an RFID badge to unlock the server-room door.
course.exam: Access badge = physical credential.
course.check_q: Which physical security mechanism commonly uses RFID to control door access?

slides.title: Lighting
slides.teach: Security lighting uses adequate illumination to make suspicious activity easier to see and less attractive to attackers.

course.learn: Security lighting uses adequate illumination to make suspicious activity easier to see and less attractive to attackers.

breakdown.explanation: Improve visibility.
Exterior lighting, parking-lot lighting, and illuminated entrances.

course.why: Lighting can deter intruders and improve camera and guard effectiveness.
course.example: A company improves lighting around a dark loading area so cameras can capture clearer images at night.
course.exam: Lighting = visibility.
course.check_q: Which physical control improves visibility for guards and cameras at night?

slides.title: Infrared Sensor
slides.teach: An infrared sensor detects infrared energy, commonly body heat or changes associated with movement.

course.learn: An infrared sensor detects infrared energy, commonly body heat or changes associated with movement.

breakdown.explanation: Detect heat.
Passive infrared motion detectors are common physical-security sensors.

course.why: Infrared detection can identify a person entering a protected area.
course.example: A sensor detects a person's body heat as they enter a room.
course.exam: Infrared = heat.
course.check_q: Which sensor commonly detects body heat?

slides.title: Pressure Sensor
slides.teach: A pressure sensor detects physical pressure or weight.

course.learn: A pressure sensor detects physical pressure or weight.

breakdown.explanation: Something stepped on or pressed it.
Pressure mats, floor sensors, and weight-sensitive pads.

course.why: Pressure sensors can reveal when someone stands on or crosses a monitored area.
course.example: A hidden mat triggers an alarm when someone steps on it.
course.exam: Pressure = weight.
course.check_q: Which sensor is activated when someone steps on a monitored mat?

slides.title: Microwave Sensor
slides.teach: A microwave sensor transmits microwave energy and detects changes caused by movement.

course.learn: A microwave sensor transmits microwave energy and detects changes caused by movement.

breakdown.explanation: Use microwave/radio energy to detect motion.
Microwave motion detectors.

course.why: These sensors can detect movement by measuring changes in reflected microwave signals.
course.example: A detector identifies movement by measuring changes in reflected microwave energy.
course.exam: Microwave = radio/motion.
course.check_q: Which sensor uses microwave energy to detect movement?

slides.title: Ultrasonic Sensor
slides.teach: An ultrasonic sensor uses high-frequency sound waves to detect movement or distance.

course.learn: An ultrasonic sensor uses high-frequency sound waves to detect movement or distance.

breakdown.explanation: Use sound to detect movement.
Ultrasonic motion and proximity sensors.

course.why: Changes in reflected sound can reveal movement in a protected space.
course.example: A sensor sends high-frequency sound waves and detects movement from the returning signal.
course.exam: Ultrasonic = sound.
course.check_q: Which sensor uses high-frequency sound waves?

slides.title: Deception Technology
slides.teach: Deception technology uses fake resources to trick attackers into interacting with something that appears real.

course.learn: Deception technology uses fake resources to trick attackers into interacting with something that appears real.

breakdown.explanation: Give attackers believable bait.
Honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles, and honeytokens.

course.why: Legitimate users usually have no reason to interact with decoys, so interaction can be a strong sign of suspicious activity.
course.example: A fake server is intentionally deployed so defenders can observe attackers who interact with it.
course.exam: Deception = trick or bait.
course.check_q: A fake server is created to attract attackers. What security approach is this?

slides.title: Disruption Technology
slides.teach: Disruption technology uses security techniques to interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

course.learn: Disruption technology uses security techniques to interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

breakdown.explanation: Interrupt what the attacker is trying to accomplish.
Redirecting malicious traffic, isolating compromised systems, and sending attackers toward decoys.

course.why: Disruption reduces an attacker's ability to communicate, move, or complete an attack.
course.example: Malware traffic is redirected away from its intended malicious destination.
course.exam: Disruption = interrupt.
course.check_q: A defender redirects malicious traffic to prevent the attacker from reaching the intended destination. Which concept applies?

slides.title: Non-repudiation
slides.teach: Non-repudiation provides proof that someone performed an action so they cannot reasonably deny doing it later.

course.learn: Non-repudiation provides proof that someone performed an action so they cannot reasonably deny doing it later.

breakdown.explanation: You cannot say you did not do it when reliable evidence ties the action to you.
Digital signatures, audit logs, timestamps, and signed transactions.

course.why: Organizations may need strong evidence showing who approved, signed, sent, or performed an important action.
course.example: A manager digitally signs a transaction and later claims they never approved it.
course.exam: Look for prove, cannot deny, signed, evidence, or proof of approval.
course.check_q: A company needs proof that a manager approved a transaction and cannot later deny it. Which concept applies?

cia.name: Confidentiality
cia.definition: Keeping information private from people who are not authorized to see it.
cia.exam_question: Was data exposed to someone who should not see it?
cia.scenario: An employee accidentally emails a customer database containing SSNs to the wrong person.

cia.name: Integrity
cia.definition: Keeping information accurate and protected from unauthorized changes.
cia.exam_question: Was data changed or tampered with?
cia.scenario: An attacker changes employees' direct-deposit bank account numbers in payroll.

cia.name: Availability
cia.definition: Making sure authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
cia.exam_question: Can authorized users access it when they need it?
cia.scenario: A DDoS attack overwhelms a website so legitimate customers cannot connect.

What should exist based on goals, standards, or requirements?
What is missing or insufficient between the current and desired states?
What should be changed to close the gap?

questions.q: A stolen laptop contains unencrypted customer records. Which CIA principle is MOST directly at risk?
questions.explanation: Confidentiality concerns unauthorized disclosure of information.

questions.q: An attacker changes product prices in an e-commerce database. Which CIA principle is compromised?
questions.explanation: Integrity is affected because data was modified without authorization.

questions.q: A DDoS attack prevents customers from reaching a company's website. Which CIA principle is MOST affected?
questions.explanation: Availability is affected because legitimate users cannot access the service.

questions.q: A user enters a password and MFA code before signing in. Which AAA function is being performed?
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who the user is.

questions.q: A signed-in employee may view reports but cannot modify them. Which AAA function determines this?
questions.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to do.

questions.q: A system records when a user logs in, which files are opened, and when the user logs out. Which AAA function is this?
questions.explanation: Accounting records and tracks user activity.

questions.q: A client validates a server's digital certificate before connecting. Which concept is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: The client is verifying the identity of a system/server.

questions.q: A company compares its current controls against a required baseline and identifies missing safeguards. What is this?
questions.explanation: Gap analysis compares the current state with the desired or required state.

questions.q: A user on the internal network must still pass identity and device checks before accessing a sensitive application. Which model is this?
questions.explanation: Zero Trust does not automatically trust a user or device based on network location.

questions.q: Which Zero Trust component evaluates context and decides whether access should be allowed?
questions.explanation: The Policy Engine makes the access decision.

questions.q: Which Zero Trust component acts on the Policy Engine's decision to establish or terminate access?
questions.explanation: The Policy Administrator carries out the Policy Engine's decision.

questions.q: Which Zero Trust component actually allows, blocks, or terminates a connection at the access point?
questions.explanation: The Policy Enforcement Point enforces the decision.

questions.q: A login from an unusual country causes the system to require additional verification. Which Zero Trust concept is this?
questions.explanation: Adaptive identity changes verification requirements based on risk and context.

questions.q: A compromised account can reach only one required application instead of the entire network. Which concept is being used?
questions.explanation: Threat scope reduction limits the blast radius of a compromise.

questions.q: Which physical control is specifically designed to stop vehicles from reaching a building?
questions.explanation: Bollards are posts or barriers designed to stop or redirect vehicles.

questions.q: A user badges through one door and must wait for it to close before the second door opens. Which control is this?
questions.explanation: An access control vestibule uses two controlled doors to regulate entry.

questions.q: A hidden mat triggers an alarm when someone steps on it. Which sensor is being used?
questions.explanation: A pressure sensor detects weight or physical pressure.

questions.q: A sensor uses high-frequency sound waves to detect movement. Which sensor is this?
questions.explanation: Ultrasonic sensors use high-frequency sound waves.

questions.q: A fake API key is planted where an attacker may find it and triggers an alert if used. What is it?
questions.explanation: A honeytoken is fake data or a credential that should never be legitimately used.

questions.q: A company needs proof that a manager approved a transaction and cannot later deny it. Which concept applies?
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation provides evidence that ties the action to the person.

flashcards.title: CIA Triad
flashcards.answer: Confidentiality = secret; Integrity = correct; Availability = accessible.
flashcards.exam: Exposed → confidentiality; changed → integrity; unavailable → availability.

flashcards.title: Non-repudiation
flashcards.answer: Proof that someone performed an action so they cannot reasonably deny it later.
flashcards.exam: Think digital signatures, audit logs, timestamps, and 'can't deny it.'

flashcards.title: AAA
flashcards.answer: Authentication = who are you? Authorization = what can you do? Accounting = what did you do?
flashcards.exam: Use the three questions to identify the correct AAA function.

flashcards.title: Authenticating people
flashcards.answer: Verifying the identity of a human user.
flashcards.exam: Think passwords, PINs, biometrics, smart cards, and MFA.

flashcards.title: Authenticating systems
flashcards.answer: Verifying the identity of a device, server, application, or service.
flashcards.exam: Think certificates, machine identities, keys, and service credentials.

flashcards.title: Authorization models
flashcards.answer: Methods that determine how permissions are assigned and evaluated.
flashcards.exam: Think role-based, attribute-based, or rule-based access.

flashcards.title: Gap analysis
flashcards.answer: Compare the current state with the desired state to identify what is missing.

flashcards.title: Zero Trust
flashcards.answer: No user, device, or connection is automatically trusted.

flashcards.title: Control Plane
flashcards.answer: The Zero Trust plane that makes access decisions.

flashcards.title: Data Plane
flashcards.answer: The Zero Trust plane where permitted traffic and resource access occur.

flashcards.title: Adaptive identity
flashcards.answer: Verification requirements change based on risk and context.
flashcards.exam: Unusual location/device/risk can trigger stronger authentication.

flashcards.title: Threat scope reduction
flashcards.answer: Limit how much damage a compromise can cause.
flashcards.exam: Think least privilege, segmentation, and 'limit the blast radius.'

flashcards.title: Policy-driven access control
flashcards.answer: Defined security policies determine whether access should be allowed.

flashcards.title: Policy Engine
flashcards.answer: Evaluates context and decides whether access should be granted.

flashcards.title: Policy Administrator
flashcards.answer: Acts on the Policy Engine's decision to establish or terminate access.

flashcards.title: Policy Enforcement Point
flashcards.answer: Actually allows, denies, or terminates the connection.

flashcards.title: Implicit trust zones
flashcards.answer: Areas where users/devices are trusted automatically based on location.
flashcards.exam: Zero Trust tries to reduce automatic internal trust.

flashcards.title: Subject/System
flashcards.answer: Subject requests access; system is the protected resource.

flashcards.title: Bollards
flashcards.answer: Strong physical barriers used to stop or redirect vehicles.

flashcards.title: Access control vestibule
flashcards.answer: A two-door controlled entry area used to regulate access.
flashcards.exam: One door closes before the next opens.

flashcards.title: Fencing
flashcards.answer: Physical perimeter barrier.

flashcards.title: Video surveillance
flashcards.answer: Cameras used to monitor and record activity.

flashcards.title: Security guard
flashcards.answer: Human physical-security control that monitors, verifies, and responds.

flashcards.title: Access badge
flashcards.answer: Physical credential used to identify a person and control entry.

flashcards.title: Lighting
flashcards.answer: Illumination used to improve visibility and deter suspicious activity.

flashcards.title: Infrared sensor
flashcards.answer: Detects infrared energy such as body heat.

flashcards.title: Pressure sensor
flashcards.answer: Detects physical pressure or weight.

flashcards.title: Microwave sensor
flashcards.answer: Uses microwave energy to detect movement.

flashcards.title: Ultrasonic sensor
flashcards.answer: Uses high-frequency sound waves to detect movement or distance.

flashcards.title: Honeypot
flashcards.answer: A fake system or service designed to attract attackers.

flashcards.title: Honeynet
flashcards.answer: A fake network with multiple decoy systems.

flashcards.title: Honeyfile
flashcards.answer: A fake file designed to reveal unauthorized interest or access.

flashcards.title: Honeytoken
flashcards.answer: Fake data or credentials that should never be legitimately used.

flashcards.title: Deception technology
flashcards.answer: Fake resources created to trick attackers.

flashcards.title: Disruption technology
flashcards.answer: Security techniques that interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow an attack.
